blocks.title: I.. INTRODUCTION
blocks.content:
Representation theory provides a powerful set of tools
for analyzing systems invariant under the action of some
group such as a molecular symmetry group in chemistry or
a gauge group in quantum ﬁeld theory. For example, the
eigenvalue spectrum of a quantum system is usually com-
puted by decomposing the Hilbert space into a direct sum
of irreducible representations of the symmetry group and
diagonalizing each irreducible block of the Hamiltonian
separately.

be viewed as a ﬁngerprint that uniquely identiﬁes the irrep

blocks.title: II.. GROUP THEORY REFRESHER
blocks.content:
Suppose that G is a ﬁnite group. A d-dimensional rep-
resentation of G is a group homomorphism from G to
the unitary group U(d). A representation is irreducible if
the ambient Hilbert space Cd contains no proper subspace
invariant under the action of all group elements. It is stan-
dard to identify irreps that diﬀer only by a basis change
in the ambient Hilbert space. Then any ﬁnite group has a
ﬁnite set of irreps. Given a group element g ∈G and an
irrep λ, let ρλ(g) be the unitary matrix corresponding to g.

blocks.title: VI.. CLASSICAL COMPLEXITY OF SAMPLING
blocks.content:
In Sec. V we showed that a quantum computer can
eﬃciently sample from probability distributions (28) and
(29) associated with a given column or row of the char-
acter table of the symmetric group Sn. Are these sampling
problems hard for classical computers?

blocks.title: A.. Granularity and quantum advantage
blocks.content:
Let us ﬁrst consider a general setting in which a sam-
pling problem is deﬁned by a probability distribution P
over some ﬁnite set  called the sample space and an
error tolerance ϵ. We consider inﬁnite families of prob-
lem instances labeled by an integer n called the problem
size. It is required that each point x ∈ can be speci-
ﬁed by poly(n) bits. Likewise, the probability distribution
P should admit a succinct classical description of size
poly(n). We also assume that the error tolerance obeys
ϵ ≥poly(1/n). A classical or quantum algorithm solves
the sampling problem if it outputs a samp

There exists a constant B > 0 such that the fraction of permutations g ∈Sn with c(g) > B log (n) cycles is at most 1/n100 for all large enough n. If c(g) ≤B log n, use the MPS algorithm to compute χλ(g), which takes time nO(log n). Otherwise, if c(g) > B log n, output some ﬁxed integer (say zero). This gives the desired algorithm. ■ Next let us consider the row sampling problem.

There exists a classical algorithm that takes as input an irrep λ of the symmetric group Sn, a permuta- tion g ∈Sn, and outputs an integer k(g) such that k(g) = χλ(g) for at least a 1 −1/n100 fraction of permutations g ∈Sn. The algorithm has runtime nO(log n).

suggests that classically hard instances of the problem can be constructed by choosing the input permu- tation g ∈Sn with a large number of cycles, for example, c(g) ∼√n. In this case best-known classical algorithms for computing the characters χλ(g) appear to require an exponential time. However, we need to check whether per- mutations g with a large number of cycles give rise to instances of the row sampling problem with a granular distribution. This is addressed in the following lemma.

blocks.title: Granularity for row sampling
blocks.content: There exist a universal constant A > 0 such that the probability distribu- tion Pg(λ) over partitions λ ⊢n from Eq. (28) is granular whenever g ∈Sn is a permutation with at most A√n/ log n cycles.

blocks.title: B.. Row and column sampling
blocks.content:
We have already seen that the column sampling prob-
lem obeys properties (1) and (2). Furthermore, computing
the probability Pλ(g) = |χλ(g)|2/n! is #P-hard in the worst
case [4]. Moreover, this problem is not contained in #P
unless the polynomial hierarchy collapses to the second
level [4]. However, it seems unlikely that average-case
hardness property (3) holds for this problem. In particu-
lar, the following lemma gives a classical quasipolynomial
time algorithm for computing Pλ(g) that succeeds with
high probability if g ∈Sn is a random permutation.

blocks.title: VII.. CLASSICAL MPS ALGORITHM FOR KOSTKA NUMBERS
blocks.content:
KOSTKA NUMBERS
In Sec. IV we showed that Crichigno and Prakash’s con-
nection between quantum spin chains and characters of the
symmetric group can be leveraged in an MPS algorithm
for characters. In Ref. [13] they also proved mappings
between spin chains and Kostka numbers and Littlewood-
Richardson coeﬃcients. Using similar ideas to characters,
we show that this correspondence can be used to give an
MPS algorithm for Kostka numbers.
